cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
We can create alternating emf by rotating a coil in a magnetic field.
Take N identical turns, area A per turn and a uniform field B.
Rotate the coil at constant angular speed omega.
Choose time zero when its normal follows the field.
Flux linkage is N B A times cosine of omega t.
Apply Faraday's law: minus the derivative of linkage gives induced emf N B A
omega times sine of omega t.
The sine appears because we differentiated the cosine.
When linkage is greatest, its instantaneous rate of change is zero, so emf is
zero.
A quarter turn later the coil's plane is parallel to the field, linkage is
zero
and its rate of change has greatest magnitude.
Emf reaches a peak.
Do not pair maximum flux with maximum emf.
The chosen starting orientation fixes our waveform phase; another time origin
changes the phase, not the amplitude.
A simple AC generator uses slip rings to maintain connection while allowing
alternating output, whereas a split ring arrangement changes the terminal
waveform.
Under load, magnetic effects resist rotation and mechanical input is needed.
An open circuit emf can exist without significant load power.
Rotation is an energy conversion mechanism, not a free electrical source.
Let's give the generator numbers.
Use one hundred turns, field zero point two tesla, area zero point zero one
square meter and angular speed one hundred radians per second.
Peak emf is N B A omega, which gives twenty volts.
Frequency is one hundred over two pi, about fifteen point nine hertz.
The ideal sinusoidal RMS emf is twenty divided by square root of two, about
fourteen point one four volts.
Pause and predict what happens if rotation speed doubles.
Peak emf doubles to forty volts, and frequency doubles to about thirty one
point eight hertz.
RMS emf also doubles.
If instead turns double at the same speed, amplitude doubles but frequency
stays unchanged.
Those are different experimental changes.
With a purely resistive ten ohm load and negligible generator internal
impedance, the first generator gives RMS current about one point four one
amperes and average power twenty watts.
A real generator's terminal voltage can depend on loading, winding resistance
and inductive effects.
Our ideal numerical example neglects those.
Do not confuse the peak twenty volts with a constant twenty volt DC supply.
Follow the same sequence each time: geometry and speed, peak waveform
amplitude, frequency, RMS conversion, then the circuit response if a load is
specified.
A transformer does not need mechanical rotation.
It uses changing magnetic flux to link a primary and secondary winding.
In the ideal model, both windings link the same core flux, and each turn has
the same induced emf magnitude.
Therefore secondary voltage over primary voltage equals secondary turns over
primary turns.
Use either RMS magnitudes throughout or peak magnitudes throughout.
If secondary turns exceed primary turns, it is a step up transformer.
If fewer, it is step down.
Take primary turns five hundred and secondary turns one hundred.
With primary RMS voltage two hundred thirty volts, ideal secondary RMS voltage
is forty six volts.
Winding orientation determines the relative terminal phase, so the turns ratio
alone is a magnitude statement unless polarity references are given.
Why not apply a steady DC supply?
After any initial transient, steady current produces steady linked flux, which
cannot sustain secondary emf.
In a real transformer, direct DC connection can cause damaging primary current
and heating because the intended alternating flux operation is absent.
This is a conceptual explanation, not a home experiment.
Core properties, insulation and ratings matter.
Transformers are designed for specified operating conditions.
Our ideal turns ratio relation assumes shared changing flux, negligible
leakage
and negligible winding voltage losses.
A higher transformer output voltage does not create extra power.
In an ideal lossless transformer, input power equals output power.
For our ideal resistive load example, primary RMS voltage times primary RMS
current equals the corresponding secondary product.
Thus current ratio is inverse to voltage ratio.
The five to one step down transformer gives forty six volts on the secondary
from two hundred thirty volts on the primary.
If the secondary supplies a two ampere resistive load, output power is ninety
two watts.
Ideal primary current is zero point four ampere.
A step down voltage can accompany increased load current because power is
conserved.
We neglect magnetising current and losses in this calculation.
With arbitrary phase shifted loads, distinguish real power from apparent
power;
do not silently drop power factors in a real efficiency calculation.
Now treat a different, real transformer with ninety two watts output and
efficiency eighty percent.
Input real power is output divided by efficiency: one hundred fifteen watts.
Losses are twenty three watts.
The ideal voltage ratio is not by itself a complete model of real voltage
regulation.
Real losses can include winding heating, eddy current heating and hysteresis.
Laminated cores reduce eddy current losses, while appropriate core materials
and design limit other losses.
State which ideal relations you are using, and which real quantity the
efficiency describes.
Let's connect transformers to transmission.
Suppose a line must carry ten kilowatts with unity power factor, and the total
line resistance is two ohms.
At a line operating voltage of one thousand volts, current is ten amperes.
Line heating is current squared times resistance: two hundred watts.
Raise the operating voltage to ten thousand volts while carrying the same
power.
Current becomes one ampere and line heating becomes two watts.
Voltage increased tenfold; line loss fell by a factor of one hundred.
The reasoning requires fixed transmitted power, the same line resistance and
the stated power factor.
It does not say that raising voltage across a fixed resistor reduces its
heating; that is a different circuit condition.
Transmission systems use step up and step down stages so long distance
currents
can be smaller while equipment receives appropriate voltages.
Real systems include transformer losses, reactive power, insulation
requirements and safety constraints.
The classroom arithmetic is not a plan for handling high voltage equipment.
Finish with three checks.
In a generator, changing coil orientation creates a flux derivative.
In a transformer, changing shared flux gives a turns ratio.
In a transmission line, current sets resistive loss.
In all three, account for the energy source and keep peak, RMS and real power
clearly labelled.
